title: Robust Aggregation for Federated Intrusion Detection under Heterogeneous Data and Model Poisoning: A Controlled Comparison on NSL-KDD
affiliation: ¹ Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, 632014, Tamil Nadu, India
abstract: Federated learning (FL) allows network nodes to train a shared intrusion detection system (IDS) without exchanging raw traffic, but its standard aggregation rule, Federated Averaging (FedAvg), is vulnerable to non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) client data and to malicious clients that submit manipulated model updates. Few papers study both problems in a single experiment, so FedAvg was compared with coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean and Krum while the neural IDS, the dataset and the partitioning code stayed identical. The NSL-KDD dataset was divided among ten simulated clients using near-IID and Dirichlet non-IID (α = 0.3) partitions, and 0%, 20% or 30% of clients submitted sign-flipped, threefold-scaled updates; every configuration was repeated over five seeds. With 30% malicious clients on near-IID data, FedAvg accuracy fell from 76.5% to 22.8%, whereas the robust rules stayed within 0.2 percentage points of their clean accuracy. On non-IID data with 20% malicious clients, FedAvg reached 60.1 ± 21.5% accuracy against 78.1–81.7% for the robust rules, but with five seeds the non-IID differences were not significant after Holm correction. An equal-weight FedAvg ablation showed that most of the robust rules' advantage on clean non-IID data comes from FedAvg's dataset-size weighting, and a trimmed mean configured for fewer attackers than were present failed (β = 0.1: 57.9% near-IID accuracy at 30% malicious clients), whereas Krum with f = 1 did not. The robust rules took 1.4 to 6.7 times FedAvg's server aggregation time, under 2 ms per round. Robust aggregation is therefore a cheap safeguard against this naive attack, although results from one dataset and one non-adaptive attack should not be generalised.
keywords: model poisoning; robust aggregation; Byzantine resilience; non-IID data; Krum; NSL-KDD

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

5G and emerging 6G networks are evolving into distributed computing and networking ecosystems that combine massive Internet-of-Things connectivity, edge computing, network virtualisation, network slicing and intelligent network management. These capabilities increase the number and diversity of participating devices and services and consequently expand the attack surface. Security mechanisms therefore need to operate across distributed environments while accounting for privacy, scalability and heterogeneous network conditions [5]–[10]. These networks motivate the present study, but the experiments below use a general network-intrusion benchmark rather than 5G/6G traffic, so the results are not claims about 5G/6G deployments (Section 5, limitation (i)).

Intrusion detection systems (IDSs) watch network traffic, usually through flow statistics, and raise an alert when they see malicious behaviour. Machine-learning-based IDSs can learn complex patterns, but conventional centralised training generally requires security data from multiple locations to be transferred to common infrastructure. In a distributed edge or IoT deployment this means extra bandwidth use, exposure of sensitive network records, and a central server that has to cope with ever more sources. Federated learning (FL) avoids this: every client keeps its own dataset and only sends model parameters or updates to a server, which merges them into one shared model [1]–[4].

Earlier papers have applied FL to IoT security with deep-learning and anomaly-detection models, and have built federated IDSs for massive IoT, software-defined networking and 5G-oriented settings [11]–[15], [20]–[22], [25]. Their results show that intrusion detection can work without gathering raw training data in one place. How well it works, though, varies with how the data are spread over clients, with the model, and with the aggregation strategy. Non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) traffic is a good example: each client sees a different mix of attacks, so the local models pull in different directions and the global model converges and generalises less well [14].

FL brings security risks of its own. A compromised participant can tamper with its local training or with the update it uploads, which may degrade the global model or push it toward behaviour the attacker wants. Work on FL security, and on AI security in 6G, repeatedly lists malicious clients, adversarial updates, privacy leakage and trust management as open problems [1], [3], [8], [18], [24]. A federated IDS therefore needs to be judged on how it copes with bad updates and on what it costs to communicate, as well as on ordinary classification metrics.

The recent literature contains substantial work on individual dimensions of this problem, including federated IDS, non-IID learning, communication-efficient FL, continual learning and adversarial threats [14], [18]–[20], [23], [24]. These dimensions are nevertheless frequently investigated using different datasets, client partitions and evaluation criteria, so the practical value of robust aggregation for IDS remains difficult to read from the published evidence.

Accordingly, this study is a controlled comparison in which the dataset, local IDS model and client partitioning are held fixed while the aggregation rule, the degree of data heterogeneity and the fraction of malicious clients are varied.
This work makes three contributions:

A reproducible controlled comparison in which raw training data remain local to ten simulated clients and four aggregation rules (FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean and Krum) can be exchanged without changing any other component; the code and the per-round logs of every run are public.

An evaluation under near-IID and Dirichlet non-IID partitions with 0%, 20% and 30% malicious clients that jointly reports detection performance, degradation under attack, convergence and server-side cost, together with two ablations: FedAvg with equal client weights, and robust rules configured for fewer attackers than are present.

An empirical finding, replicated over five seeds, that FedAvg lost 53.7 accuracy points on near-IID data with 30% malicious clients while the robust rules lost at most 0.2 points; that under non-IID data the robust rules' advantage over FedAvg without an attacker is mostly explained by FedAvg's size weighting; and that trimmed mean, unlike Krum here, fails when its trimming level is set below the attacker fraction.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 describes the problem formulation and methodology. Section 4 presents the experimental results. Section 5 discusses the findings and limitations, and Section 6 concludes.
2. Literature Review
2.1 Federated learning for cybersecurity and privacy

Federated learning supports decentralised model training without requiring all training examples to be collected by a single server. Security and privacy surveys show that FL can reduce direct sharing of raw data, but model updates can still expose information and can themselves become attack surfaces [1]–[4]. This is especially relevant to IoT and distributed network environments, where data are generated close to devices and edge nodes. The literature therefore treats communication efficiency, client heterogeneity, trust and adversarial robustness as important complements to the basic privacy advantage of FL [2], [3]. The reference algorithm for most of this work is Federated Averaging, in which clients train locally and the server averages their models in proportion to local dataset size [26].
2.2 Federated IDS in IoT and 5G/6G

Ferrag et al. tested several neural architectures for federated IoT cybersecurity on a range of security datasets [11]. Mothukuri et al. used FL for anomaly detection against IoT attacks [12]. FELIDS is a federated IDS for agricultural IoT that was evaluated on several intrusion-detection datasets [22], and IDSoft is a federated, softwarised IDS for massive IoT in a 6G setting that pays attention to convergence and communication overhead [13]. Two recent papers cover federated DDoS detection in large-scale software-defined networks [25] and a mixture-of-experts federated IDS for 5G and IoT [20]. All of these show that FL can be applied to distributed IDS. They differ, however, in what they set out to measure and in how their experiments are set up.
2.3 Heterogeneity, communication cost and adversarial robustness

Different nodes in a network see different traffic volumes, applications and attack classes, so heterogeneity matters a great deal for intrusion detection. Djaidja et al. compared FedAvg, FedProx, FedPer and SCAFFOLD for 5G and beyond intrusion detection on IID and non-IID data, and their results highlight the influence of data distribution and FL algorithm choice [14]. A common way to generate controlled heterogeneity in such experiments is to draw each client's class proportions from a Dirichlet distribution, whose concentration parameter sets the degree of skew [31]. Communication-efficient on-device FL has also been investigated in industrial IoT [21]. In parallel, adversarial-security research for AI-driven 6G systems highlights the risks posed by manipulated learning processes [8]. Recent surveys of FL for 5G/6G cybersecurity and FL-based IDS further identify malicious clients, aggregation vulnerabilities, privacy and communication efficiency as continuing challenges [18], [24].

Outside the IDS literature, a dedicated line of work addresses malicious participants through the aggregation rule. Krum selects the single client update that lies closest to its nearest neighbours and was proposed to tolerate Byzantine workers [27]. Coordinate-wise median and trimmed mean combine updates dimension by dimension and discard extreme values, and have been analysed in terms of statistical error rates [28]. Conversely, model-poisoning attacks that boost a malicious update, and attacks crafted specifically against Byzantine-robust rules, have been shown to degrade FL models [29], [30], [33], [34]. Whether these general-purpose rules still work on intrusion-detection traffic, where client distributions are strongly skewed, is what this paper tests.
2.4 Newer, more specialised work

Newer papers use more specialised designs. One applies generative techniques to imbalanced industrial-IoT IDS data [15]; another proposes continual federated learning for attacks that keep evolving in SDN-based edge computing [19]; a third studies few-shot learning for classifying attack traffic when labelled examples are scarce [23]. Post-quantum and blockchain-enhanced FL have also been looked at [17], and broader 6G surveys list the security requirements of future intelligent networks [5], [6], [9], [16]. These designs show how wide the field is, but each extra component makes it harder to see what the aggregation rule alone contributes.
2.5 Research gap

Taken together, the cited work shows that FL can support distributed intrusion detection, and other papers separately cover non-IID data, 5G/6G security, communication efficiency and adversarial threats. What is still missing is a single, controlled and reproducible comparison of IDS performance, degradation under malicious clients, aggregation robustness and communication overhead under the same conditions (Table 1). To fill that gap, the dataset, local IDS model, client-partition strategy and metrics are held fixed here, and only the aggregation mechanism and the poisoning condition change. The contribution is a comparative experiment. It is not a claim that federated IDS or robust aggregation is itself a new idea.

blocks.text: 3. Methodology
3.1 Problem formulation

In a distributed network the security data sit on many different devices and edge nodes, and training an IDS centrally on them is often undesirable because of data transfer, privacy, scalability and communication limits. Federated learning can reduce the need to centralise raw traffic by allowing local training and collaborative model aggregation. Two characteristics of realistic distributed environments challenge this approach: client datasets are often non-IID because different network nodes observe different traffic and attack distributions, and participating clients may be compromised and submit manipulated model updates. Under these conditions, conventional FedAvg may produce a less reliable global IDS model. Robust aggregation can reduce the influence of abnormal updates but may introduce additional computational or communication costs. The problem addressed here is therefore to determine how the choice of aggregation rule influences detection performance, resilience to malicious clients, convergence and communication overhead under heterogeneous network-traffic distributions.

Let there be K clients, where client k holds a local dataset Dₖ of nₖ labelled flows and n = Σₖ nₖ. The IDS is a binary classifier f(x; w) with parameter vector w that returns the probability that a flow x is an attack. The federated objective is
min_w F(w) = Σₖ₌₁..K (nₖ / n) Fₖ(w),   Fₖ(w) = (1 / nₖ) Σ₍ₓ,ᵧ₎∈Dₖ L( f(x; w), y )

where L is the binary cross-entropy loss. In round t the server broadcasts wᵗ, each client trains locally to obtain wₖᵗ and returns the update Δₖᵗ = wₖᵗ − wᵗ. A malicious client replaces its honest update with a scaled sign-flipped one,
Δ′ₖᵗ = −γ Δₖᵗ
with scale γ = 3, and the server then computes the next global model as
wᵗ⁺¹ = wᵗ + A( Δ₁ᵗ, …, Δ_Kᵗ )

where A is the aggregation rule under study. Four rules were compared. FedAvg weights each update by dataset size, A_avg = Σₖ (nₖ / n) Δₖ [26]. Coordinate-wise median takes, for every parameter index j, the median of Δₖ,ⱼ across clients [28]. Trimmed mean sorts the K values of each coordinate, discards the m = ⌊βK⌋ smallest and m largest, and averages the remaining K − 2m [28]. Krum assigns each client the score
s(k) = Σᵢ∈Nₖ ‖ Δₖ − Δᵢ ‖²

where Nₖ contains the K − f − 2 clients nearest to k, and returns the single update with the lowest score [27]. In the main experiments β = 0.3 (m = 3) and f = 3. Two further variants were used only as ablations (Section 4.5): equal-weight FedAvg, A_eq = (1/K) Σₖ Δₖ, which differs from FedAvg only in ignoring dataset size; and trimmed mean with β = 0.1 (m = 1) and Krum with f = 1, i.e. defences configured for one attacker when three are present. Detection quality was measured on the attack class as accuracy, precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN) and F1 = 2·precision·recall/(precision+recall).
3.2 Data

The NSL-KDD dataset was used [32]. It contains 125,973 training records (KDDTrain+) and 22,544 test records (KDDTest+), each described by 41 features and a label. The files were obtained from a public GitHub mirror of the dataset (github.com/defcom17/NSL_KDD). Three categorical features (protocol type, service and flag) were one-hot encoded, giving 122 input features, and all features were standardised with a scaler fitted on the training set only. The one-hot column set was derived from the union of training and test records so that both sets share one feature space; no labels were involved. Labels were binarised as normal (0) or attack (1). The training set contained 46.5% attack records and KDDTest+ 56.9%. Training attacks were also grouped into four categories (DoS 45,927, Probe 11,656, R2L 995 and U2R 52 records, against 67,343 normal records) solely to create non-IID partitions. KDDTest+ contains attack types that do not occur in the training set, so absolute accuracies in this study are bounded by that distribution shift. The data are public and contain no human or animal subjects, so no ethics approval was required.

The training set was distributed over K = 10 clients with the Dirichlet procedure of [31]: for each of the five categories, client proportions were drawn from Dir(α) and records were allocated accordingly; a draw was repeated in the rare case that a client received fewer than 128 records (one mini-batch). A concentration of α = 100 produced near-IID shards (for seed 0, between 11,544 and 13,562 records per client, with 42–49% attacks), and α = 0.3 produced strongly heterogeneous shards (for seed 0, between 2,686 and 41,928 records, attack share between 2% and 100%, and the most frequent category making up 53–100% of a client's data). The two settings are denoted near-IID and non-IID below.
3.3 Simulation procedure

The simulation (Figure 1) runs synchronous FL on one machine. Each run proceeded as follows: (i) the server initialised a global model; (ii) in every round all ten clients received the global model and trained it locally on their own shard; (iii) a randomly chosen subset of clients, fixed for the whole run and sized 0%, 20% or 30% of K, replaced its update according to Eq. (2); (iv) the server aggregated the updates with one of the rules in Eq. (3); and (v) the new global model was evaluated on KDDTest+ and the statistics were logged. Raw records never left their client; only parameter updates were exchanged. The server was assumed to see each client's individual update, which the three robust rules require. No secure aggregation, differential privacy, or attacker adaptation to the aggregation rule was modelled.

blocks.text: 3.4 Experimental setup

The local IDS was a multilayer perceptron with 122 inputs, one hidden layer of 64 ReLU units and one sigmoid output (7,937 parameters), initialised with He-normal weights. Local training used mini-batch SGD with batch size 128, learning rate 0.05 and one local epoch per round, for 25 communication rounds. These values were set before the experiments and were not tuned on the test set. Every combination of partition (near-IID, non-IID), malicious fraction (0%, 20%, 30%) and aggregation rule (the four main rules plus equal-weight FedAvg) was run with five seeds (0–4), and the two misconfigured defences were run at 30% malicious clients on both partitions, giving 170 runs. The seed fixed the initial weights, the partition, the choice of malicious clients and the order of mini-batches, so all rules saw identical conditions for a given seed.

No validation split was held out, and validation-based early stopping was not used: every run trained for 25 rounds and the reported figures are those of the final round, so no model selection on test data occurred. Because median and trimmed mean reach their highest accuracy after one or two rounds on non-IID data and then decline (Section 4.3), Table 5 also reports the best-round accuracy of each run. That figure is chosen with knowledge of the test set and is shown only to quantify how much final-round reporting understates the peak; it is not a deployable result.

Server aggregation time was measured around the aggregation call only, as the mean over rounds. Uplink volume was computed from the update size. Differences between each robust rule and FedAvg in final accuracy were tested with a two-sided Welch t-test over the five seeds; the twelve p-values in Table 4 were adjusted with the Holm step-down procedure [35], and effect sizes are given as Cohen's d with pooled standard deviation [36]. Experiments ran on a CPU-only cloud workspace with two virtual cores using Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5.3, pandas 3.0.5, SciPy 1.18.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1 and Matplotlib 3.11.2; the MLP and the federated loop were implemented directly in NumPy, and scikit-learn was used only for scaling and metrics.
4. Results
4.1 Detection performance and resilience to malicious clients

Table 2 reports final-round performance on KDDTest+ for the near-IID partition and Table 3 for the non-IID partition; Figure 2 summarises accuracy. Values are mean ± standard deviation over five seeds. With no attacker on near-IID data the four rules were indistinguishable: accuracy lay between 76.3% and 76.5%. With 20% malicious clients FedAvg was unaffected on average (76.8%), but with 30% its accuracy collapsed to 22.8 ± 1.9% and its F1 to 35.5%, a loss of 53.7 points. Median, trimmed mean and Krum stayed between 76.2% and 76.3% at the same attack level, within 0.2 points of their clean accuracy.

blocks.caption: Table 2. Final-round performance on KDDTest+, near-IID partition (α = 100). Values are mean ± standard deviation over five seeds (recall and precision: mean). Attack is the positive class. FedAvg (equal wt.) is the equal-weight ablation of Section 4.5.

blocks.text: On the non-IID partition (Table 3) the picture was different even without an attacker. FedAvg reached 75.6 ± 0.8% accuracy and 62.4% attack recall, whereas median and trimmed mean reached 78.1% and 77.8% accuracy with recall of 67.7% and 67.0%, at essentially unchanged precision (about 92%). Section 4.5 shows that most of this gap disappears when FedAvg weights clients equally. Krum had the highest mean recall (78.8%) but also the largest run-to-run spread (76.4 ± 11.7% accuracy), because in one of five seeds (seed 3) it converged to a model that labelled every test flow as an attack (accuracy 56.9%, equal to the attack share of KDDTest+).

With attackers present on non-IID data, FedAvg degraded by 15.5 points at 20% and 25.6 points at 30% malicious clients, and its F1 fell to 56.0 ± 25.8% and 50.4 ± 13.0%. Its variance was very high: at 20% malicious clients final accuracy ranged from 28.2% to 76.5% across seeds, depending on which clients were compromised. The robust rules ended at 78.1–81.7% (20%) and 78.2–80.6% (30%), with standard deviations between 2.1 and 4.7 points.

Figure 2. Final-round test accuracy (%) versus the fraction of malicious clients for the four aggregation rules on the near-IID (left) and non-IID (right) partitions. Each bar shows the mean of five seeds, and the error bars show one standard deviation. Hatching distinguishes rules so the figure remains legible in greyscale.

blocks.text: 4.2 Statistical comparison

Table 4 gives the difference in mean final accuracy between each robust rule and FedAvg, the Welch t-test p-value (n = 5 per group) before and after Holm correction over the twelve comparisons, and Cohen's d. On near-IID data with 30% malicious clients the differences exceeded 53 points with p < 0.001 after correction, while at 20% they were below 0.5 points and not significant. On non-IID data the robust rules were 18–31 points ahead of FedAvg and the effect sizes were large (d = 1.2–2.0), but the differences were not statistically significant: at 20% malicious clients the unadjusted p-values were 0.09–0.13, and at 30% they were 0.030–0.040 before correction and 0.27–0.31 after it. Put plainly, the non-IID differences at 30% are significant only before multiple-comparison correction, and those at 20% not even then; with five seeds and FedAvg's large seed-to-seed variance the study is underpowered for the non-IID comparisons.

blocks.caption: Table 4. Difference in mean final accuracy (percentage points) between each robust rule and FedAvg, with two-sided Welch t-test p-values before and after Holm correction over the twelve comparisons, and Cohen's d (pooled standard deviation). Five seeds per group.
blocks.note: The very large d values on near-IID data at 30% reflect the small within-group spread of both groups rather than an especially meaningful effect size.

blocks.text: 4.3 Convergence

Accuracy curves are shown in Figure 3 (non-IID) and Figure 4a (near-IID, 30% malicious). In all clean near-IID runs the models reached their plateau within the first one or two rounds; later rounds changed accuracy by less than about one point. On clean non-IID data, median and trimmed mean averaged 80.9% and 81.0% accuracy after round 1 and then declined to 78.1% and 77.8% by round 25, whereas FedAvg rose from 73.3% to 75.6%. Table 5 quantifies this: on clean non-IID data the best-round accuracy of median and trimmed mean was 82.9% and 81.4%, reached on average in round 1.6 and 1.2, against 78.1% and 77.8% in the final round. With malicious clients on non-IID data FedAvg curves stayed far below the robust curves in every round. Table 5 also gives the mean accuracy over all 25 rounds and the first round at which a run reached 74% accuracy, together with the number of runs (of five) that reached it at all. At 30% malicious clients, FedAvg never reached 74% on either partition, while every robust run did.

blocks.text: 4.4 Communication and server cost

Every rule exchanged the same payload. Each client uploaded one update of 7,937 float32 parameters, i.e. 31,748 bytes (31.0 KiB) per round, so ten clients produced 310 KiB per round and 7.6 MiB over 25 rounds in the uplink direction, with an identical downlink for the broadcast model. The rules therefore did not differ in communication volume. They differed in server computation (Figure 4b): mean aggregation time per round, over all main configurations, was 0.256 ms for FedAvg, 0.355 ms for Krum, 0.918 ms for trimmed mean and 1.730 ms for median, i.e. 1.4, 3.6 and 6.7 times the FedAvg cost. Krum was implemented with a single Gram-matrix computation of all pairwise distances, which makes it cheap at K = 10; its cost grows quadratically with the number of clients, whereas the cost of median and trimmed mean grows with the model dimension (and as K log K per coordinate). These differences are small in absolute terms for a model of this size.

blocks.caption: Figure 4. (a) Test accuracy (%) per round on the near-IID partition with 30% malicious clients (mean ± one standard deviation over five seeds). (b) Mean server aggregation time per round in milliseconds across all main configurations; error bars show one standard deviation.

blocks.text: 4.5 Ablations: equal-weight FedAvg and misconfigured defences

Equal-weight FedAvg. To test whether the robust rules beat FedAvg on clean non-IID data because FedAvg weights clients by dataset size, FedAvg was rerun with equal client weights (A_eq in Section 3.1). On clean non-IID data it reached 77.1 ± 0.3% accuracy, 1.5 points above size-weighted FedAvg (75.6%; Welch p = 0.007), with recall rising from 62.4% to 65.4% at unchanged precision. This closes 60% of the gap to median and 68% of the gap to trimmed mean, and the remaining differences between equal-weight FedAvg and median or trimmed mean were not significant (Welch p = 0.29 and 0.23). On near-IID data, where shards are of similar size, the two FedAvg variants coincided (76.5% each). Equal weighting gave no protection against the attack: with 20% and 30% malicious clients on non-IID data it reached 60.0% and 48.9%, and on near-IID data at 30% it collapsed to 23.3% (Tables 2 and 3).

Misconfigured defences. The main experiments set β = 0.3 and f = 3, which equal the largest attacker fraction and so assume that the defender knows it. Table 6 reports the same 30% attack against trimmed mean with β = 0.1 (one value trimmed from each end of every coordinate) and Krum with f = 1. Trimmed mean failed: accuracy fell to 57.9 ± 12.3% on near-IID and 64.7 ± 9.7% on non-IID data, against 76.2% and 78.2% when correctly configured, because with three attackers and m = 1 at least two scaled values survive in every coordinate. It still did better than FedAvg (22.8% and 50.0%). Krum with f = 1 was unaffected on near-IID data (76.5 ± 0.5%) and lost 3.6 points on non-IID data (77.1 ± 3.7%). With f = 1 Krum scores each update by its distance to its seven nearest neighbours; the three malicious updates are inflated, point in different directions and are therefore far from everything, so an honest update still has the lowest score. This tolerance is specific to an attack whose malicious updates do not agree with each other; colluding attackers that submit similar updates would not be rejected this way [30], [33], [34]. Median has no tuning parameter and tolerates any minority of attackers by construction.

blocks.caption: Table 6. Misconfigured defences against 30% malicious clients: final-round performance on KDDTest+ (mean ± standard deviation over five seeds; recall and precision: mean). The last column repeats the accuracy of the correctly configured rule (β = 0.3 or f = 3) from Tables 2 and 3.

blocks.text: 5. Discussion

The near-IID result has a simple mechanical explanation. With equal-sized shards and a fraction ρ of clients sending −γΔ, the FedAvg step along the honest direction is approximately (1 − ρ) − ργ = 1 − ρ(1 + γ). For γ = 3 this equals +0.2 at ρ = 0.2 and −0.2 at ρ = 0.3. At 20% the honest signal therefore survives, only shrunk, which is consistent with the unchanged accuracy, and at 30% the aggregate step points away from the honest direction and the model is driven to a worse-than-chance state (FedAvg accuracy of 22.8% is below the 43.1% obtained by predicting every flow as normal). The scaled updates produce extreme coordinate values, which median and trimmed mean simply ignore, and Krum rejects the whole update as an outlier. None of the three was therefore affected, provided the malicious clients stayed a minority within the trimming or Krum tolerance used here; Section 4.5 shows that trimmed mean is not protected when that tolerance is set too low. This analysis is an interpretation of the numbers and was not tested separately, for example by varying γ.

Under non-IID data the situation is less clean. First, FedAvg weights clients by dataset size, so a single large client can dominate. In the seed-0 partition one client held 33% of all records, which means the outcome depends heavily on whether that client is a malicious one. This fits the very wide spread of FedAvg accuracy at 20% (28.2%–76.5%). Second, the robust rules outperformed FedAvg even with no attacker. The equal-weight ablation (Section 4.5) supports the size-weighting explanation: giving every client the same weight raised FedAvg's clean non-IID accuracy by 1.5 points and its recall by 3.1 points, leaving no significant difference from median or trimmed mean. Small, attack-heavy shards therefore carry useful signal that size weighting suppresses, and median-type rules recover it because they treat clients more equally. The residual gap of about one point may also reflect that KDDTest+ has a higher attack share (56.9%) than the training data (46.5%), which favours rules that are less biased toward the majority class. Median and trimmed mean peak after round 1 or 2 at about 81% and then fall to about 78%, which looks like continued fitting to the training distribution. Since only final-round results are reported, the effect pulls the reported figures down rather than up; Table 5 gives the size of the gap.

The results are consistent with the studies cited in Section 2 on two points: data heterogeneity can change how FL algorithms rank against each other [14], and aggregation vulnerabilities are a real concern for FL-based IDS [18], [24]. They also agree with the original analyses of Krum and coordinate-wise rules [27], [28]. It should be stated explicitly that the attack tested here, a scaled sign flip, is exactly the kind of large, outlying update that these three rules were designed to reject, so their success against it is expected rather than surprising. The study does not test attacks crafted to evade such rules: the boosted and targeted model poisoning of Bhagoji et al. [29], the local model poisoning attacks of Fang et al. [30], A Little Is Enough (ALIE), which hides small coordinated perturbations inside the honest variance [33], and the min-max and min-sum attacks of Shejwalkar and Houmansadr [34]. The absence of degradation observed here should therefore not be read as evidence of robustness to adaptive attackers. Direct numerical comparison with other NSL-KDD studies is not meaningful because the present model, partitioning and test protocol differ, and KDDTest+ accuracy for a plain MLP is limited by its unseen attack types.

For practitioners the results suggest that, for models of this size, replacing FedAvg by a robust rule costs at most about 1.5 ms of server time per round and no extra communication, and removed the catastrophic failure in every attacked setting that was tested. The price is that the server must see each client's update individually, which is typically incompatible with secure aggregation. Each rule also has a specific weakness: trimmed mean must be configured for at least the true attacker fraction, and Krum, by selecting one client's update per round, can be unstable under strong heterogeneity (one of five clean non-IID runs collapsed to predicting only attacks). In this study coordinate-wise median, which needs no estimate of the attacker fraction, looks like the safest default. Krum gave the best mean accuracy under attack but was the least predictable from seed to seed. Where no attack is expected, equal-weight FedAvg recovers most of the robust rules' clean non-IID advantage at the lowest cost.

This study has limits that readers should keep in mind. (i) NSL-KDD is the only dataset. It is a general network-intrusion benchmark from 2009, not a 5G/6G dataset, so the 5G/6G motivation in Section 1 rests on the structural similarity of distributed, heterogeneous traffic sources and not on real 5G/6G traces. (ii) A single attack was tested, a scaled sign flip with γ fixed at 3, which is the attack the three robust rules were designed to reject; the attacker never adapted to the aggregation rule, and the attacks of [29], [30], ALIE [33] and min-max/min-sum [34] remain untested, as do data-poisoning attacks such as label flipping. (iii) The IDS was a small MLP that reaches its plateau within one or two rounds, so the convergence and cost comparisons say little about larger models; ten clients participated in every round, and the malicious fraction was limited to 30%. Only one misconfigured setting per rule was tested. (iv) Five seeds give low statistical power: after Holm correction none of the non-IID differences in Table 4 is significant, although the effect sizes are large. (v) The partition and the choice of malicious clients were random, which introduces large variance in the non-IID experiments. (vi) Absolute accuracies are limited by the distribution shift in KDDTest+, and no validation split was used for early stopping. These limitations mean that the findings show the behaviour of these rules in a controlled setting and do not establish it for operational deployments.
6. Conclusion

This study compared FedAvg with coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean and Krum for federated intrusion detection on NSL-KDD under near-IID and non-IID client partitions and with 0%, 20% and 30% malicious clients. FedAvg lost 53.7 accuracy points on near-IID data with 30% malicious clients, whereas the robust rules changed by at most 0.2 points. On non-IID data with 20% malicious clients FedAvg reached 60.1% accuracy against 78.1–81.7% for the robust rules, a large but, with five seeds, not statistically significant difference after correction. Most of the robust rules' advantage on clean non-IID data was explained by FedAvg's size weighting, and trimmed mean failed when configured for fewer attackers than were present. The robust rules required the same communication volume as FedAvg and 1.4 to 6.7 times its server aggregation time, still under 2 ms per round. This contributes a reproducible, controlled comparison of aggregation rules for federated IDS under heterogeneity and poisoning, with public code and per-run results. Future work will repeat the protocol on datasets that contain 5G/6G traffic, add adaptive attacks such as ALIE and min-max and data-poisoning attackers, vary the scale of the attack and the number of clients, use more seeds, and evaluate secure-aggregation-compatible defences.
